about: ELEC0005 is a 15-credit first-year UCL module taught in Term 2 that gives the physics behind electronic engineering: electromagnetism (vector description of E and B fields, the integral forms of Maxwell's equations, Gauss's and Faraday's laws, and why field analysis matters beyond circuit voltages and currents) and the physics of semiconductors, applied to diodes, LEDs, solar cells and transistors. The 2026/27 catalogue lists in-person teaching and assessment of 70% exam and 30% coursework (three assessments). The catalogue gives a description rather than a numbered syllabus, so this topic list is built from that description, taking the electromagnetism material first and then the semiconductor and device material.
topics: Why field analysis matters beyond circuit voltages and currents
Vector notation for electric and magnetic fields: flux and circulation
Gauss's law for electric fields and capacitance
Magnetic fields: Gauss's law for magnetism and the Ampère–Maxwell law
Faraday's law and induction in devices
Maxwell's equations in integral form and electromagnetic waves
Semiconductor fundamentals: energy bands, carriers and doping
Carrier transport: drift, diffusion and conductivity
Transistors: MOSFET and BJT operating principles

notes.body:
Circuit theory describes a system with voltages between nodes and currents in wires. That works brilliantly when the circuit is small and slow, but it is an approximation of the underlying electromagnetic fields. This module starts by explaining when the approximation holds and why engineers sometimes need the fields themselves.

Charges, forces and fields
- Coulomb's law: two point charges q₁, q₂ a distance r apart in vacuum repel or attract with force F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r²), where 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 8.99 × 10⁹ N m²/C².
- Example: two 1 nC charges 1 cm apart feel F ≈ 8.99 × 10⁹ × 10⁻¹⁸/10⁻⁴ ≈ 9.0 × 10⁻⁵ N.
- The electric field is force per unit charge, E = F/q (units V/m or N/C). A point charge q produces E = q/(4πε₀r²), pointing radially away from a positive charge. A 1 nC charge gives about 9.0 × 10⁴ V/m at 1 cm.
- The electrostatic potential V (volts) is potential energy per unit charge. The potential difference between two points is minus the line integral of E between them; for a uniform field across a gap d, V = E d.
- Energy unit for devices: 1 electron-volt (eV) is the energy gained by an electron crossing 1 V, about 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

When circuit theory is enough
- Lumped-element circuit theory assumes signals travel instantly across the circuit. This is fine when the circuit is much smaller than the wavelength λ = v/f of the signals.
- At 50 Hz, λ in free space is about 6000 km, so a building's wiring is "small". At 1 GHz, λ ≈ 30 cm in free space and less on a circuit board, so a 5 cm track is a significant fraction of a wavelength. A common rule of thumb is that interconnects longer than roughly a tenth of a wavelength must be treated as transmission lines.

Why fields matter to an electronic engineer
- Coupling and interference: fields from one conductor induce voltages in another (crosstalk, mains hum, electromagnetic compatibility).
- Radiation: antennas, wireless links and unwanted emissions exist only because changing fields propagate as waves.
- Breakdown and insulation: dry air breaks down at roughly 3 MV/m (approximate), so the field, not just the voltage, sets how close conductors can be.
- Devices: inside transistors and diodes, carriers respond to local fields in depletion regions and across nanometre-thin gate oxides; a 1 V drop across 10 nm is a field of 10⁸ V/m.
- Components themselves: capacitance and inductance are defined by the stored electric and magnetic fields.

Superposition
Electric fields from several charges add as vectors, so the field of a charge distribution is the vector sum (or integral) of the contributions of its parts.

Exam tips: always state the condition for the lumped approximation (size ≪ wavelength); keep track of vector direction when adding fields; convert cm and nm to metres before using ε₀.


Approximate constants used in this pack: e ≈ 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, ε₀ ≈ 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, μ₀ ≈ 4π × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 1.257 × 10⁻⁶ H/m, c ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, k_B ≈ 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, kT/q ≈ 25.9 mV at 300 K.

notes.h: Vector description of fields: flux and circulation
notes.body:
Electric and magnetic fields have both magnitude and direction at every point, so they are vector fields. Maxwell's equations in integral form are written using two kinds of integral of these fields: flux through a surface and circulation around a loop.

Vector basics
- A vector in Cartesian form: A = A_x x̂ + A_y ŷ + A_z ẑ, magnitude |A| = √(A_x² + A_y² + A_z²).
- Dot product: A·B = |A||B| cos θ = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z. It is a scalar and picks out the component of one vector along another.
- Cross product: A × B has magnitude |A||B| sin θ and direction given by the right-hand rule; x̂ × ŷ = ẑ.
- Lorentz force on a charge q moving with velocity v: F = q(E + v × B). The magnetic part is perpendicular to v, so it changes direction but does no work. Example: an electron at 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to 0.1 T feels a force of about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ N.
- Field lines: E lines start on positive charge and end on negative charge; B lines form closed loops.

Line integrals and circulation
- ∫ E · dl along a path adds up the component of E along each small step dl.
- The potential difference is V(b) − V(a) = −∫ from a to b of E · dl. For electrostatic fields this is independent of path.
- Around a closed loop the integral is written ∮ E · dl and called the circulation. For static charges it is zero; Faraday's law says it equals −dΦ_B/dt when magnetic flux changes.
- ∮ B · dl around a loop relates to the current threading the loop (Ampère's law).

Surface integrals and flux
- Flux of B through a surface: Φ_B = ∫ B · dA, where dA is a small area element with direction normal to the surface. Unit: weber (Wb = T m²).
- For a uniform field through a flat area: Φ = B A cos θ, θ being the angle between B and the surface normal. Example: 0.5 T at 60° to the normal through 0.02 m² gives 0.5 × 0.02 × 0.5 = 5 mWb.
- For a closed surface, ∮ means integrate over the whole surface with dA pointing outwards. Net outward electric flux measures enclosed charge (Gauss's law); net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero.

Using symmetry
The integral laws are most useful when symmetry makes the field constant in magnitude over a chosen surface or path, so it can come outside the integral:
- Spherical symmetry (point charge): use a concentric sphere, area 4πr².
- Cylindrical symmetry (long wire or line charge): use a coaxial cylinder or circle, circumference 2πr.
- Planar symmetry (large sheet, parallel plates): use a "pillbox" box crossing the sheet.

Differential versions of the same laws (divergence and curl) exist, but this module uses the integral forms, which connect directly to measurable quantities such as charge, current and voltage.

Exam tips: draw the Gaussian surface or Ampèrian loop on your sketch, state the symmetry argument that makes the field constant on it, and watch the angle in B·A (between B and the normal, not the surface).

Gauss's law links the electric field to the charge that produces it. With symmetry it gives fields in a few lines, and it underpins the capacitor formulas used throughout electronics.

Statement (integral form)
- In vacuum: ∮ E · dA = Q_enc/ε₀. The net outward electric flux through any closed surface equals the total charge enclosed divided by ε₀.
- Charges outside the surface contribute zero net flux (field lines enter and leave).
- In a dielectric it is convenient to use the electric flux density D = ε₀ε_r E (for a linear, isotropic material) and write ∮ D · dA = Q_free,enc, so only free charge appears.

Standard results (vacuum; replace ε₀ by ε₀ε_r inside a dielectric)
- Point charge or spherical charge (outside it): E = Q/(4πε₀r²) — the Gaussian surface is a sphere, E·4πr² = Q/ε₀.
- Infinite line charge λ (C/m): E = λ/(2πε₀r) — coaxial cylinder of length L, E·2πrL = λL/ε₀.
- Infinite sheet of surface charge σ (C/m²): E = σ/(2ε₀) on each side — pillbox through the sheet.
- Two parallel plates with ±σ: fields add between the plates, E = σ/ε₀, and cancel outside (ideal, edge effects ignored).
- Inside a uniformly charged spherical shell: E = 0 (no charge enclosed).

Conductors in electrostatics
- The field inside a conductor is zero once charges have settled; any excess charge sits on the surface.
- Just outside the surface the field is normal to it with magnitude σ/ε₀.
- A closed conducting enclosure shields its interior from external static fields (Faraday cage).

Capacitance
- For parallel plates of area A and separation d with a dielectric ε_r: E = σ/(ε₀ε_r), V = E d, Q = σA, so C = Q/V = ε₀ε_r A/d.
- Energy stored: ½CV², equivalently an energy density ½ε₀ε_r E² in the field.
- Device example: a MOS gate with silicon dioxide (ε_r ≈ 3.9), thickness 10 nm and area 1 μm² has C ≈ 3.9 × 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 10⁻¹²/10⁻⁸ ≈ 3.5 fF. The capacitance per area, ε_ox/t_ox ≈ 3.45 × 10⁻³ F/m², is what lets the gate control the channel charge.
- Thinner dielectrics and higher ε_r give more capacitance per area, which is why chip makers moved to "high-k" gate dielectrics.

Physical interpretation
Gauss's law is the field form of "charges are the sources of E". Field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative ones, and the number of lines crossing a closed surface counts the charge inside.

Exam tips: always state the symmetry and the Gaussian surface; write the left-hand side as E × (area) explicitly; remember the factor of 2 difference between a single sheet (σ/2ε₀) and a parallel-plate capacitor (σ/ε₀).


Approximate constants used in this pack: e ≈ 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, ε₀ ≈ 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, μ₀ ≈ 4π × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 1.257 × 10⁻⁶ H/m, c ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, k_B ≈ 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, kT/q ≈ 25.9 mV at 300 K.

notes.h: Magnetic fields: no monopoles, and Ampère's law with Maxwell's correction
notes.body:
Magnetic fields are produced by moving charges (currents) and by changing electric fields. Two of Maxwell's equations describe this.

Gauss's law for magnetism
- ∮ B · dA = 0 for any closed surface.
- Meaning: there are no isolated magnetic poles (monopoles). Every B field line that enters a closed surface also leaves it, so magnetic field lines form closed loops.
- Practical consequence: the flux into one end of a transformer core equals the flux out of the other; flux is conserved round a magnetic circuit.

Ampère's law (static currents)
- ∮ B · dl = μ₀ I_enc: the circulation of B around a closed loop equals μ₀ times the current threading the loop. Direction by the right-hand grip rule.
- In magnetic materials it is convenient to use H, with B = μ₀μ_r H, and write ∮ H · dl = I_free,enc.

Standard results (vacuum or air unless μ_r is given)
- Long straight wire: a circle of radius r gives B × 2πr = μ₀I, so B = μ₀I/(2πr). Example: 10 A at 5 cm gives B = 4 × 10⁻⁵ T = 40 μT, comparable to the Earth's field (very roughly 25–65 μT depending on location).
- Long solenoid with n turns per metre: B = μ₀ n I inside, about zero outside. Example: 1000 turns/m and 2 A give about 2.5 mT. A ferromagnetic core multiplies this by μ_r (until saturation).
- Toroid with N turns: B = μ₀ N I/(2πr) inside the core, zero outside.

The displacement-current correction
Ampère's law in the static form fails for a charging capacitor: a loop around the wire is threaded by current I, but a surface bulging between the plates is threaded by no conduction current, even though the loop is the same. Maxwell resolved this by adding the displacement current:
- ∮ B · dl = μ₀ I_enc + μ₀ε₀ dΦ_E/dt, where Φ_E = ∫ E · dA.
- Between capacitor plates, ε₀ dΦ_E/dt = ε₀ A dE/dt = dQ/dt = I, so the displacement current exactly matches the conduction current in the wires.
- This term means a changing electric field creates a magnetic field. Together with Faraday's law it allows self-sustaining electromagnetic waves.

Forces
- On a current-carrying wire: F = I L × B, magnitude BIL sin θ. This is the motor effect.
- Two parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction attract.

Where this shows up in devices
Inductors and transformers (field set by winding current), current sensors, magnetic shielding, and the parasitic inductance of PCB tracks and bond wires.

Exam tips: draw the Ampèrian loop and say why B is constant along it; include μ_r when there is a core; for capacitor questions show explicitly that the displacement current equals the wire current.


Approximate constants used in this pack: e ≈ 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, ε₀ ≈ 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, μ₀ ≈ 4π × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 1.257 × 10⁻⁶ H/m, c ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, k_B ≈ 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, kT/q ≈ 25.9 mV at 300 K.

notes.h: Faraday's law and induction in devices
notes.body:
Faraday's law describes how a changing magnetic flux produces an electric field and hence an EMF. It is the operating principle of transformers, generators, inductors and many sensors.

Statement
- Integral form: ∮ E · dl = −dΦ_B/dt, where Φ_B = ∫ B · dA is the magnetic flux through any surface bounded by the loop.
- For a coil of N turns linking the same flux: EMF ε = −N dΦ/dt.
- Lenz's law (the minus sign): the induced EMF drives current in the direction that opposes the change of flux that caused it. This is energy conservation in action.
- The flux can change because B changes (transformer EMF), because the loop moves or changes area in a field (motional EMF, ε = B L v for a rod of length L moving at v perpendicular to B), or both.

Consequence for circuit theory
An induced electric field is not conservative: its circulation around a loop is non-zero. Strictly, Kirchhoff's voltage law only holds when no changing flux threads the loop. Circuit theory handles this by "lumping" the changing flux into inductors and assigning them a voltage L di/dt.

Worked examples
- Changing field: a 100-turn coil of area 10 cm² (10⁻³ m²) sees B fall uniformly from 0.5 T to 0 in 10 ms. |ε| = N A ΔB/Δt = 100 × 10⁻³ × 0.5/0.01 = 5 V.
- AC generator: an N-turn coil of area A rotating at angular speed ω in a uniform field B has flux linkage NΦ = NBA cos ωt, so ε = NBAω sin ωt, peak NBAω. With N = 50, B = 0.2 T, A = 0.01 m² and 50 Hz (ω = 2π × 50), the peak EMF is 50 × 0.2 × 0.01 × 314 ≈ 31.4 V.

Self-inductance
- L = NΦ/I (flux linkage per unit current), so v = L di/dt follows from Faraday's law.
- Long solenoid: L = μ₀μ_r N²A/l. Example: 100 turns, A = 1 cm², l = 5 cm, air core gives about 25 μH.
- Mutual inductance couples two windings sharing flux.

Ideal transformer
- Both windings link the same core flux Φ, so V₁ = N₁ dΦ/dt and V₂ = N₂ dΦ/dt, giving V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁.
- Power balance (ideal, lossless) gives I₂/I₁ = N₁/N₂.
- Transformers only work with changing flux; a DC voltage applied to a winding produces no steady secondary voltage.

Eddy currents
Changing flux induces circulating currents in conducting cores, wasting power as heat. Laminated or ferrite cores reduce them. The same effect is used deliberately in induction heating and eddy-current braking.

Exam tips: compute flux first (with the cos θ), then its rate of change; use Lenz's law to give the direction in words; for rotating coils remember ε_peak = NBAω with ω in rad/s.

notes.h: Maxwell's equations in integral form and electromagnetic waves
notes.body:
The four Maxwell equations together describe all classical electromagnetic behaviour. In integral form each one links a field integral to a measurable source.

The four equations (vacuum, integral form)
1. Gauss's law: ∮ E · dA = Q_enc/ε₀. Charges are sources and sinks of E.
2. Gauss's law for magnetism: ∮ B · dA = 0. No magnetic monopoles; B lines close on themselves.
3. Faraday's law: ∮ E · dl = −dΦ_B/dt. A changing magnetic flux induces a circulating E.
4. Ampère–Maxwell law: ∮ B · dl = μ₀ I_enc + μ₀ε₀ dΦ_E/dt. Currents and changing electric flux produce a circulating B.
In linear materials the source terms are often written with D = εE and H = B/μ, so that only free charge and free current appear. These equations, together with the Lorentz force F = q(E + v × B), are the complete classical picture.

Connections to circuit elements
- Capacitor: Gauss's law → C = εA/d; displacement current carries the "current" across the gap.
- Inductor and transformer: Ampère's law gives B from the winding current; Faraday's law gives the voltage.
- Resistor: not from Maxwell's equations alone; it needs the material law J = σE (Ohm's law in field form).

Electromagnetic waves
- In empty space (no charges or currents) Faraday's law says a changing B creates E, and the displacement term says a changing E creates B. The two sustain each other and travel as a wave.
- Speed in vacuum: c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. Maxwell recognised this as the measured speed of light, identifying light as an electromagnetic wave.
- In a non-magnetic dielectric (μ_r ≈ 1): v = c/√ε_r, and the refractive index n = √ε_r. For ε_r = 4, v = c/2 ≈ 1.5 × 10⁸ m/s, so signals on a circuit board travel noticeably slower than in air.
- A plane wave in vacuum has E and B perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel (transverse), with |E| = c|B|.
- The Poynting vector S = E × H gives the power flow per unit area (W/m²) and its direction.
- Wavelength λ = v/f: in vacuum about 3 m at 100 MHz and 12.5 cm at 2.4 GHz.

The electromagnetic spectrum
Radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet and X-rays are all the same phenomenon at different frequencies. Visible light spans roughly 400–700 nm; this matters later for LEDs and solar cells, where photon energy E = hf = hc/λ links light to semiconductor band gaps.

Exam tips: be able to write all four integral equations from memory with correct signs and constants, and say in words what each one means and where it appears in a real device; derive c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) numerically as a check.


Approximate constants used in this pack: e ≈ 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, ε₀ ≈ 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, μ₀ ≈ 4π × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 1.257 × 10⁻⁶ H/m, c ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, k_B ≈ 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, kT/q ≈ 25.9 mV at 300 K.

notes.h: Semiconductors: energy bands, carriers and doping
notes.body:
The second half of the module turns to the materials electronic devices are made from. The key ideas are energy bands, two kinds of mobile carrier, and doping.

Energy bands
- In a crystal, the discrete energy levels of isolated atoms broaden into bands. The highest band filled with electrons at 0 K is the valence band; the next band up is the conduction band. The energy gap between them is the band gap E_g.
- Metals have a partly filled band (or overlapping bands), so electrons move freely.
- Insulators have a large gap (silicon dioxide about 9 eV, approximate), so almost no electrons are excited across it.
- Semiconductors have a moderate gap, so at room temperature a small number of electrons are thermally excited into the conduction band.
- Approximate band gaps at 300 K: Si 1.12 eV, Ge 0.66 eV, GaAs 1.42 eV, GaN 3.4 eV. Silicon has an indirect gap; GaAs and GaN have direct gaps (important for light emission).

Electrons and holes
- An electron excited to the conduction band leaves behind an empty state in the valence band, a hole. A hole behaves as a positive carrier of charge +e.
- Both carry current: electrons in the conduction band, holes in the valence band.

Intrinsic semiconductors
- In pure material n = p = n_i, the intrinsic carrier concentration.
- For silicon at 300 K, the modern accepted value is n_i ≈ 1.0 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³; many older textbooks use 1.5 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³. Both appear in exam papers, so use the value the question gives and state which one you use; answers in this pack use 1.0 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ unless stated otherwise. Silicon has about 5 × 10²² atoms/cm³, so there is only about one intrinsic electron for every 5 × 10¹² atoms.
- n_i rises very steeply with temperature, roughly as T^(3/2) exp(−E_g/2kT), and is much smaller for wide-gap materials.

Doping (extrinsic semiconductors)
- Donors: group V atoms (phosphorus, arsenic) in silicon have a fifth valence electron that is easily released at room temperature, making n-type material with electrons as majority carriers.
- Acceptors: group III atoms (boron) accept an electron from the valence band, creating holes; p-type material.
- At room temperature dopants are essentially fully ionised, so for N_D ≫ n_i, n ≈ N_D (and for N_A ≫ n_i, p ≈ N_A).

Mass-action law
- In thermal equilibrium (non-degenerate doping), n p = n_i².
- Example: silicon with N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ at 300 K: n ≈ 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ and p = n_i²/n = 10²⁰/10¹⁶ = 10⁴ cm⁻³ (using n_i = 1.0 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³; with 1.5 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ it would be 2.25 × 10⁴ cm⁻³). Doping raises the majority concentration and suppresses the minority one.

Fermi level
- The Fermi level E_F marks the energy at which the occupation probability is one half. In intrinsic material it lies near mid-gap (the intrinsic level E_i).
- n-type doping moves E_F towards the conduction band: E_F − E_i = kT ln(n/n_i). For the example above, E_F − E_i ≈ 0.0259 × ln(10⁶) ≈ 0.36 eV (about 0.35 eV with n_i = 1.5 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³). p-type doping moves it towards the valence band.

Exam tips: state "thermal equilibrium" and "300 K" when using n p = n_i²; quote which n_i value you use; remember that doping changes carrier numbers by many orders of magnitude while changing the atom count negligibly.

notes.h: Carrier transport: drift, diffusion and conductivity
notes.body:
Current in a semiconductor flows by two mechanisms: drift in an electric field and diffusion down a concentration gradient. Device behaviour depends on the balance between them.

Drift and mobility
- In a field E, carriers accelerate but keep colliding with lattice vibrations (phonons) and impurities, so they reach an average drift velocity v_d = μE (electrons move opposite to E, holes along it).
- Mobility μ (cm²/V s) measures how easily a carrier moves. Approximate room-temperature values for lightly doped silicon: μ_n ≈ 1400 cm²/V s, μ_p ≈ 450 cm²/V s. Electrons are about three times more mobile than holes, one reason n-channel transistors are preferred for speed.
- Mobility falls at higher doping (more impurity scattering) and at higher temperature (more phonon scattering).
- At very high fields the drift velocity saturates (about 10⁷ cm/s in silicon, approximate), so v = μE no longer holds.

Conductivity
- Drift current density: J = q(nμ_n + pμ_p)E = σE, which is Ohm's law in field form.
- Conductivity σ = q(nμ_n + pμ_p); resistivity ρ = 1/σ; resistance of a bar R = ρL/A.
- Intrinsic silicon (n = p ≈ 10¹⁰ cm⁻³): σ ≈ 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10¹⁰ × (1400 + 450) ≈ 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ S/cm, so ρ ≈ 3.4 × 10⁵ Ω cm (with the older n_i = 1.5 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³, σ ≈ 4.4 × 10⁻⁶ S/cm and ρ ≈ 2.3 × 10⁵ Ω cm).
- n-type silicon with N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³, taking μ_n ≈ 1200 cm²/V s at this doping (approximate): σ ≈ 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10¹⁶ × 1200 ≈ 1.9 S/cm, so ρ ≈ 0.52 Ω cm. Doping lowers resistivity by about six orders of magnitude; the hole term is negligible.

Diffusion
- Carriers spread from high to low concentration by random thermal motion.
- Electron diffusion current density: J_n = qD_n dn/dx. Hole diffusion current density: J_p = −qD_p dp/dx. The signs differ because holes are positive: both carriers diffuse down their gradient, but their charges are opposite.
- The total current density for each carrier is drift plus diffusion: J_n = qnμ_nE + qD_n dn/dx, and similarly for holes.

Einstein relation
- D/μ = kT/q (non-degenerate semiconductor). At 300 K, kT/q ≈ 25.9 mV, so D_n ≈ 1400 × 0.0259 ≈ 36 cm²/s.
- It connects diffusion and drift because both are limited by the same scattering.

Generation, recombination and diffusion length
- Excess minority carriers (from light or injection across a junction) recombine with an average lifetime τ.
- They diffuse an average distance L = √(Dτ) before recombining. With D_n = 36 cm²/s and τ = 1 μs, L = √(36 × 10⁻⁶) cm = 0.006 cm = 60 μm.
- Diffusion length determines how far injected carriers travel in diodes and how much of a solar cell can collect light-generated carriers.

Exam tips: keep units consistent (cm and cm² are standard in semiconductor work; convert carefully if mixing with SI); say which mobility value you assume; remember the minority-carrier term usually contributes negligibly to conductivity in doped material.

Joining p-type and n-type material creates a p–n junction, the building block of diodes, LEDs, solar cells and bipolar transistors.

Formation and the depletion region
- When p and n regions meet, electrons diffuse from n to p and holes from p to n, recombining near the junction.
- This leaves behind uncompensated ionised dopants: negative acceptor ions on the p side and positive donor ions on the n side. This space-charge or depletion region is almost free of mobile carriers.
- The charge creates an electric field pointing from n to p, which drives a drift current opposing the diffusion. In equilibrium drift and diffusion balance exactly and there is no net current.
- The associated potential step is the built-in potential: V_bi = (kT/q) ln(N_A N_D/n_i²).
- Example (Si, 300 K, N_A = 10¹⁷ cm⁻³, N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³, n_i = 10¹⁰ cm⁻³): V_bi = 0.0259 × ln(10³³/10²⁰) ≈ 0.0259 × 29.9 ≈ 0.77 V. (With n_i = 1.5 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ the same junction gives about 0.75 V.)
- The depletion width W ∝ √(V_bi − V_applied) and extends mainly into the more lightly doped side (charge neutrality: N_A x_p = N_D x_n). For the example W ≈ 0.33 μm, about 90 % of it on the n side.

Bias
- Forward bias (p positive relative to n) lowers the barrier, so diffusion current increases exponentially: carriers are injected across the junction as minority carriers and recombine.
- Reverse bias raises the barrier and widens the depletion region; only a small reverse saturation current I_S flows, from thermally generated minority carriers.

The ideal diode (Shockley) equation
- I = I_S [exp(V/(nV_T)) − 1], where V_T = kT/q ≈ 25.9 mV at 300 K and n is the ideality factor (1 for an ideal diode, up to about 2 in practice).
- For n = 1, current rises by a factor of 10 for every V_T ln 10 ≈ 60 mV increase in forward voltage (at 300 K).
- Example (V_T = 25.9 mV): I_S = 10⁻¹⁴ A gives about 0.115 mA at 0.6 V and about 5.5 mA at 0.7 V. This is why silicon diodes appear to "turn on" at roughly 0.6–0.7 V.
- In reverse bias (V ≪ −V_T), I ≈ −I_S.
- I_S is strongly temperature dependent (it scales with n_i²), so forward voltage at fixed current falls by roughly 2 mV/°C in silicon (approximate).

Breakdown and capacitance
- At large reverse bias the junction breaks down: Zener tunnelling in heavily doped junctions (low breakdown voltage) or avalanche multiplication (higher voltages). Zener diodes use this as a voltage reference.
- The depletion region acts as a voltage-dependent capacitor (C_j = εA/W), used in varactor diodes for tuning.

Exam tips: sketch the band diagram, charge density, field and potential across the junction; state 300 K and the n_i value you use; remember the ideal equation ignores series resistance, recombination in the depletion region and breakdown.

LEDs and solar cells are both p–n junctions that exchange energy with light. An LED converts current into photons; a solar cell converts photons into current.

Photon energy and wavelength
- E = hf = hc/λ. Handy form: λ (nm) ≈ 1240/E (eV) (hc ≈ 1240 eV nm, approximate).
- Visible light spans roughly 400–700 nm (about 3.1 to 1.8 eV).

Light-emitting diodes
- Under forward bias, electrons are injected into the p side and holes into the n side. When an electron recombines with a hole radiatively it emits a photon with energy close to the band gap.
- Emission wavelength ≈ 1240/E_g nm. GaAs (E_g ≈ 1.42 eV) emits about 870 nm, in the infrared; a material with a gap of about 1.9 eV emits red (about 650 nm); GaN (≈ 3.4 eV) emits ultraviolet near 365 nm, and InGaN alloys with smaller gaps give blue and green.
- Direct-gap materials are needed for efficient emission: in an indirect-gap material such as silicon, recombination also needs a phonon to conserve momentum, so non-radiative processes dominate and silicon makes very poor LEDs.
- An LED's forward voltage is roughly comparable to E_g/q (red LEDs about 2 V, blue about 3 V, approximate), which is why LED forward drops vary with colour.
- White LEDs commonly use a blue LED with a yellow-emitting phosphor.

Solar cells (photovoltaics)
- A photon with energy above E_g creates an electron–hole pair. Photons below E_g pass through; energy above E_g is lost as heat as carriers relax to the band edges.
- Pairs generated in or within about a diffusion length of the depletion region are separated by the built-in field: electrons to the n side, holes to the p side. This gives a photocurrent I_L flowing out of the p terminal into the external circuit.
- Cell equation (generator convention): I = I_L − I_0[exp(V/V_T) − 1].
- Short-circuit current I_sc ≈ I_L. Open-circuit voltage V_oc = V_T ln(I_L/I_0 + 1). Example: I_L = 35 mA, I_0 = 10⁻¹² A at 300 K gives V_oc ≈ 0.0259 × ln(3.5 × 10¹⁰) ≈ 0.63 V.
- Maximum power P_max = FF × V_oc × I_sc, where the fill factor FF (typically about 0.7–0.85) measures how "square" the I–V curve is.
- Efficiency η = P_max/P_in. Standard test conditions use 1000 W/m² (100 mW/cm²), AM1.5 spectrum, 25 °C.
- Example: V_oc = 0.6 V, J_sc = 35 mA/cm², FF = 0.8 gives 16.8 mW/cm² from 100 mW/cm², so η = 16.8 %.
- A single-junction cell is limited to about 33 % efficiency under unconcentrated sunlight (the Shockley–Queisser limit, approximate, best near E_g ≈ 1.3–1.4 eV), because of sub-gap losses and thermalisation. Silicon's gap of 1.12 eV absorbs wavelengths shorter than about 1.1 μm.

Photodiodes
The same physics run in reverse bias gives a photodetector: the photocurrent is proportional to light intensity.

Exam tips: use λ ≈ 1240/E_g; state test conditions for efficiency; explain why direct gaps are needed for LEDs but silicon is fine (if thick enough) for absorbing light in solar cells.

notes.h: Transistors: how MOSFETs and BJTs work
notes.body:
Transistors use a small control signal to govern a much larger current, acting as switches in digital circuits and amplifiers in analogue ones. The module introduces both main types from the physics already covered.

The MOSFET (n-channel enhancement type)
- Structure: a p-type substrate with heavily doped n⁺ source and drain regions; between them a gate electrode separated from the silicon by a thin oxide.
- The gate, oxide and silicon form a capacitor with capacitance per area C_ox = ε_ox/t_ox. A positive gate voltage repels holes and attracts electrons to the surface. Above the threshold voltage V_T the surface inverts, forming an n-type channel linking source to drain.
- Almost no DC current flows into the gate (it is insulated), so a MOSFET draws negligible static input current.

Long-channel square-law model (valid for long channels, ignoring channel-length modulation, velocity saturation and subthreshold current)
- Cut-off: V_GS < V_T, I_D ≈ 0.
- Triode (linear) region, V_GS > V_T and V_DS < V_GS − V_T: I_D = μ_nC_ox(W/L)[(V_GS − V_T)V_DS − V_DS²/2]. For small V_DS the channel behaves as a resistor controlled by V_GS.
- Saturation, V_GS > V_T and V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T: the channel pinches off at the drain end and I_D = ½μ_nC_ox(W/L)(V_GS − V_T)², nearly independent of V_DS.
- Transconductance in saturation: g_m = ∂I_D/∂V_GS = 2I_D/(V_GS − V_T).
- Example: μ_nC_ox = 200 μA/V², W/L = 10, V_T = 0.5 V, V_GS = 1.5 V in saturation: I_D = 0.5 × 200 × 10⁻⁶ × 10 × 1² = 1 mA and g_m = 2 × 1 mA/1 V = 2 mS.
- p-channel MOSFETs are the complement (n-type substrate, holes in the channel, negative V_GS). CMOS logic pairs n- and p-channel devices so that, ideally, no static current flows in either logic state.
- Thinner oxides raise C_ox and hence drive current, which links back to Gauss's law and capacitance.

The bipolar junction transistor (npn)
- Three regions: emitter (heavily doped n), thin base (p), collector (n).
- Forward-active mode: base–emitter junction forward biased, base–collector junction reverse biased.
- Electrons are injected from the emitter into the base; because the base is thin compared with the electron diffusion length, most diffuse across without recombining and are swept into the collector by the reverse-biased junction's field.
- Collector current: I_C = I_S exp(V_BE/V_T), the same exponential law as a diode.
- Current gain: I_C = βI_B, with β typically around 100 (varies widely). I_E = I_C + I_B, and α = I_C/I_E = β/(β + 1), just below 1.
- Transconductance g_m = I_C/V_T, about 38.6 mS at 1 mA and 300 K, higher than a MOSFET at the same current.

Switch versus amplifier
- As switches, transistors move between cut-off and a low-resistance state (triode for MOSFETs, saturation for BJTs; note the naming clash).
- As amplifiers they are biased in saturation (MOSFET) or forward-active (BJT), where small input changes cause proportional output-current changes, g_m × v_in.

Exam tips: always check which region a MOSFET is in by comparing V_DS with V_GS − V_T before choosing a formula; explain why a thin base gives high β; do not confuse BJT "saturation" with MOSFET "saturation".

Electric flux density D = ε₀ε_r E (linear isotropic dielectric); ∮ D · dA = free charge enclosed.

I_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt; in a charging capacitor it equals the conduction current in the leads.

L = μ₀μ_r N²A/l.

cards.f: Why does KVL fail with changing flux?
cards.b: The induced electric field is non-conservative: ∮ E · dl = −dΦ/dt ≠ 0. Circuit theory accounts for it by assigning inductors a voltage L di/dt.
Insulated laminations break up eddy-current paths, reducing eddy-current losses.
∮E·dA = Q/ε₀; ∮B·dA = 0; ∮E·dl = −dΦ_B/dt; ∮B·dl = μ₀I + μ₀ε₀ dΦ_E/dt.

cards.f: Speed of EM waves in vacuum
Wave speed in a non-magnetic dielectric
cards.b: v = c/√ε_r; refractive index n = √ε_r.

cards.f: Relationship between E and B in a vacuum plane wave
cards.b: Perpendicular to each other and to the propagation direction, with |E| = c|B|.
S = E × H: power flow per unit area (W/m²) and its direction.

cards.f: Which Maxwell term makes EM waves possible in empty space?
cards.b: The displacement current term μ₀ε₀ dΦ_E/dt, which lets a changing E field create B, complementing Faraday's law.
The energy gap E_g between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band. Si ≈ 1.12 eV, GaAs ≈ 1.42 eV at 300 K (approx.).
An empty electron state in the valence band that behaves as a mobile positive charge +e.

cards.f: Intrinsic carrier concentration of Si at 300 K
cards.b: About 1 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ (older texts often use 1.5 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³).
n p = n_i² in thermal equilibrium (non-degenerate semiconductor).
Group V elements such as phosphorus or arsenic: each supplies an extra electron, making n-type material.
Group III elements such as boron: each accepts an electron, creating a hole and making p-type material.
Direct (GaAs, GaN): electron can drop across the gap emitting a photon efficiently. Indirect (Si): needs a phonon too, so light emission is weak.

cards.f: Fermi level shift with n-type doping
cards.b: E_F − E_i = kT ln(n/n_i): moves towards the conduction band as donor concentration rises.
v_d = μE at low fields; saturates at high fields (about 10⁷ cm/s in Si, approx.).
σ = q(nμ_n + pμ_p); resistivity ρ = 1/σ.

cards.f: Typical mobilities in lightly doped Si at 300 K
cards.b: μ_n ≈ 1400 cm²/V s, μ_p ≈ 450 cm²/V s (approximate; both fall with doping and temperature).
J_n = qD_n dn/dx (for holes J_p = −qD_p dp/dx).
D/μ = kT/q; at 300 K kT/q ≈ 25.9 mV.
L = √(Dτ): average distance an excess minority carrier diffuses before recombining.

cards.f: Why does mobility fall at high doping?
cards.b: Ionised dopant atoms scatter carriers (impurity scattering), shortening the mean time between collisions.
V_bi = (kT/q) ln(N_A N_D/n_i²); e.g. about 0.77 V for N_A = 10¹⁷, N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ in Si at 300 K.
Region around the junction depleted of mobile carriers, containing ionised dopant charge that creates the built-in field.
I = I_S[exp(V/(nV_T)) − 1], V_T = kT/q ≈ 25.9 mV at 300 K; n = 1 ideally.

cards.b: V_T ln 10 ≈ 60 mV for each tenfold increase in current.

cards.f: Which side does the depletion region extend into?
cards.b: Mainly the more lightly doped side, since N_A x_p = N_D x_n.
Zener: tunnelling across a narrow depletion region in heavily doped junctions (low voltages). Avalanche: impact ionisation multiplying carriers (higher voltages).
Drift current from the built-in field exactly balances diffusion current for each carrier type; net current is zero.

questions.q: What is the magnitude of the electric field 1 cm from a 1 nC point charge in vacuum?
questions.why: E = kq/r² = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁹/(10⁻²)² ≈ 9.0 × 10⁴ V/m. About 900 V/m divides by r instead of r², which gives the potential (in volts) rather than the field. About 9.0 × 10⁻⁵ is the force in newtons between two such charges, not the field of one. About 9.0 × 10⁸ V/m uses r = 10⁻⁴ m, applying the squared conversion factor to r and then squaring again.

questions.q: For which of these is ordinary lumped circuit theory least reliable?
options: A 5 cm PCB track carrying a 2 GHz clock
A 5 cm wire carrying 50 Hz mains current
A 10 m audio cable carrying 1 kHz
A 2 m cable carrying a 10 kHz sensor signal
questions.why: At 2 GHz the free-space wavelength is 15 cm, and on a PCB less, so a 5 cm track is a large fraction of a wavelength and must be treated with field/transmission-line methods. A 5 cm mains wire is tiny compared with the 6000 km wavelength at 50 Hz. A 10 m audio cable at 1 kHz is negligible against a 300 km wavelength. A 2 m cable at 10 kHz is likewise tiny against 30 km; long length alone does not matter, the ratio to wavelength does.

questions.q: Give four reasons why an electronic engineer needs to analyse electric and magnetic fields rather than only circuit voltages and currents.
markScheme: High-frequency/size effects: lumped model fails when size is comparable to wavelength
Coupling/interference: crosstalk and EMC from fields linking conductors
Radiation and antennas: propagating waves are field phenomena
Device physics or insulation: fields in depletion regions, gate oxides, breakdown limits
questions.modelAnswer: First, lumped circuit theory assumes the circuit is much smaller than the wavelength; at GHz frequencies tracks become transmission lines and fields must be analysed. Second, fields from one conductor couple into others, causing crosstalk and electromagnetic compatibility problems that no circuit diagram shows. Third, radio links, antennas and unwanted emissions rely on fields propagating as waves. Fourth, inside devices and insulation the local field matters: carriers are swept by fields in depletion regions, gate oxides must withstand very high fields, and breakdown depends on field strength, not voltage alone.

questions.q: A uniform 0.5 T field makes an angle of 60° with the normal to a flat 0.02 m² loop. What is the flux through the loop?
questions.why: Φ = BA cos θ = 0.5 × 0.02 × cos 60° = 5 mWb. 10 mWb ignores the angle (cos θ = 1). 8.7 mWb uses sin 60° instead of cos 60°, measuring the angle from the plane of the loop rather than from its normal. 0.25 Wb is B × cos 60° with the area left out.

questions.q: An electron moves at 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a uniform 0.1 T magnetic field. Which statement is correct?
options: The force is about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ N and increases the electron's speed
The force is about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ N and changes only the direction of motion
The force is zero because B is perpendicular to v
The force is about 1.6 × 10⁻²⁰ N because only the charge and field matter
questions.why: |F| = qvB = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10⁶ × 0.1 ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ N, and because F = qv × B is perpendicular to v it does no work, so speed is unchanged and only direction changes. Saying it increases speed confuses magnetic with electric force. Saying it is zero confuses the cross product (maximum at 90°) with the dot product (zero at 90°). 1.6 × 10⁻²⁰ N drops the velocity from qvB.

questions.q: Explain the difference between the flux of a vector field through a surface and the circulation of a vector field around a loop, giving one Maxwell equation that uses each.
markScheme: Flux: surface integral ∫F·dA, adds normal component over a surface
Circulation: closed line integral ∮F·dl, adds tangential component around a loop
Flux example: Gauss's law ∮E·dA = Q_enc/ε₀ (or ∮B·dA = 0)
Circulation example: Faraday ∮E·dl = −dΦ_B/dt (or Ampère–Maxwell)
questions.modelAnswer: Flux is a surface integral, ∫ F · dA: it adds up the component of the field normal to each small piece of a surface, measuring how much field passes through it. Circulation is a closed line integral, ∮ F · dl: it adds the component of the field along each step around a closed path, measuring how much the field 'swirls' around it. Gauss's law, ∮ E · dA = Q_enc/ε₀, uses flux through a closed surface; Faraday's law, ∮ E · dl = −dΦ_B/dt, uses circulation around a loop.

questions.q: A MOS capacitor has an SiO₂ layer (ε_r ≈ 3.9) 10 nm thick and area 1 μm². Its capacitance is closest to:
questions.why: C = ε₀ε_r A/d = 3.9 × 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 10⁻¹²/10⁻⁸ ≈ 3.5 × 10⁻¹⁵ F = 3.5 fF. 0.89 fF omits ε_r (vacuum gap). 0.35 fF takes 10 nm as 100 nm (10⁻⁷ m), a thickness-conversion slip. 35 fF uses 1 nm for the thickness instead of 10 nm.

questions.q: Using Gauss's law, what is the field at distance r from a very long straight wire carrying charge λ per metre?
questions.why: A coaxial cylinder of radius r and length L encloses λL; E × 2πrL = λL/ε₀ gives E = λ/(2πε₀r). λ/(4πε₀r²) is the point-charge result, which uses a sphere where a cylinder is needed. λ/(2ε₀) has the form of the infinite-sheet result, which applies to planar symmetry. λ/(ε₀r) misses the 2π circumference of the cylinder.

questions.q: Use Gauss's law to derive the capacitance of an ideal parallel-plate capacitor with plate area A, separation d and a dielectric of relative permittivity ε_r. State the assumptions.
markScheme: Assume plates large compared with d, ignore edge (fringing) fields; uniform field between plates
Pillbox Gaussian surface enclosing part of one plate: D·A' = σA' gives D = σ, E = σ/(ε₀ε_r)
Field zero outside/inside conductor so only one face contributes
V = E d = σd/(ε₀ε_r); Q = σA
C = Q/V = ε₀ε_r A/d
questions.modelAnswer: Assume the plates are large compared with d so the field between them is uniform and fringing at the edges can be ignored. Take a pillbox whose one face lies inside the positive plate (where E = 0) and the other in the gap; only the gap face, of area A', carries flux. Gauss's law with D gives D A' = σA', so D = σ and E = σ/(ε₀ε_r). The potential difference is V = E d = σd/(ε₀ε_r) and the charge is Q = σA, so C = Q/V = ε₀ε_r A/d.

questions.q: What is the magnetic flux density 5 cm from a long straight wire carrying 10 A in air?
questions.why: B = μ₀I/(2πr) = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 10/(2π × 0.05) = 4 × 10⁻⁵ T = 40 μT. 200 μT is μ₀I/(2πr) with r = 1 cm, i.e. taking 5 cm as 0.01 m. 20 μT uses 4π instead of 2π in the denominator. 126 μT is μ₀I/(2r), the formula for the centre of a circular loop of radius r, not for a straight wire.

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor is being charged by a current of 2 mA. What is the displacement current between its plates?
options: It depends on the plate area
Zero, because no charge crosses the gap
questions.why: Between the plates ε₀ dΦ_E/dt = ε₀A dE/dt = dQ/dt, which equals the 2 mA in the leads; this is exactly why Maxwell's term makes Ampère's law consistent. Zero confuses displacement current with conduction current. 2 mA × ε₀ misreads the definition: ε₀ multiplies the rate of change of electric flux, not the current. Plate area cancels out because E = Q/(ε₀A), so the result does not depend on it.

questions.q: A long air-cored solenoid has 2000 turns per metre and carries 0.5 A. Find B inside. A soft-iron core with μ_r = 500 is then inserted; find the new B (assuming no saturation) and state one limitation of this result.
markScheme: With core: B = μ_r μ₀ n I ≈ 0.63 T
Limitation: iron saturates (around 1.5–2 T) and μ_r is not constant
Also assumes long solenoid, uniform field, ignores ends
questions.modelAnswer: B = μ₀ n I = 1.257 × 10⁻⁶ × 2000 × 0.5 ≈ 1.26 × 10⁻³ T. With the core, B = μ_r μ₀ n I ≈ 500 × 1.26 mT ≈ 0.63 T. This assumes μ_r is constant; in reality μ_r of iron varies with field and the core saturates at roughly 1.5–2 T, beyond which extra current adds little B. It also assumes an ideal long solenoid with negligible end effects.

questions.q: A 100-turn coil of area 10 cm² is in a uniform field that falls steadily from 0.5 T to zero in 10 ms. What is the magnitude of the induced EMF?
questions.why: |ε| = N A ΔB/Δt = 100 × 10⁻³ m² × 0.5 T/0.01 s = 5 V. 0.05 V leaves out the 100 turns. 500 V converts 10 cm² to 0.1 m² by dividing by 100 (the length factor) instead of 10⁴. 50 V takes the time as 1 ms instead of 10 ms.

questions.q: An ideal transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns, with 230 V rms on the primary and a 2.3 A rms secondary current. What is the primary current?
questions.why: Secondary voltage = 230 × 100/2000 = 11.5 V; power balance gives I₁ = I₂ N₂/N₁ = 2.3 × 100/2000 = 0.115 A (11.5 × 2.3 ≈ 230 × 0.115). 46 A applies the turns ratio the wrong way round (I₂ × N₁/N₂). 2.3 A assumes current is the same on both sides. 0.0058 A divides by the turns ratio twice.

questions.q: A coil of 50 turns and area 0.01 m² rotates at 50 revolutions per second in a uniform 0.2 T field. Derive the EMF as a function of time and find its peak and rms values. Explain using Lenz's law why a loaded generator is harder to turn.
markScheme: Φ per turn = BA cos ωt with ω = 2π × 50 ≈ 314 rad/s
ε = −N dΦ/dt = NBAω sin ωt
Lenz: load current creates a field/torque opposing the rotation, so mechanical work must be supplied
questions.modelAnswer: With ω = 2π × 50 ≈ 314 rad/s, the flux through each turn is Φ = BA cos ωt, so ε = −N dΦ/dt = NBAω sin ωt. The peak is 50 × 0.2 × 0.01 × 314 ≈ 31.4 V and the rms value 31.4/√2 ≈ 22.2 V. When a load draws current, that current flows in a direction that opposes the change of flux (Lenz's law); the force on the current-carrying coil produces a torque opposing rotation, so the prime mover must supply mechanical work equal to the electrical energy delivered.

questions.q: A signal travels along a long transmission line in a non-magnetic dielectric with ε_r = 4. What is its speed?
questions.why: v = c/√ε_r = 3.0 × 10⁸/2 = 1.5 × 10⁸ m/s. 7.5 × 10⁷ m/s divides by ε_r instead of its square root. 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s ignores the dielectric. 6.0 × 10⁸ m/s multiplies by √ε_r, which would exceed the speed of light.

questions.q: Which Maxwell equation in integral form expresses the fact that there are no isolated magnetic poles?
questions.why: Zero net magnetic flux through every closed surface means B lines never start or end, so there are no monopoles. ∮ E · dA = Q_enc/ε₀ is Gauss's law for electric charge. ∮ E · dl = −dΦ_B/dt is Faraday's law of induction. The Ampère–Maxwell law relates the circulation of B to currents and changing electric flux, not to monopoles.

questions.q: Write down the four Maxwell equations in integral form and, for each, name one electronic component or effect whose behaviour it explains.
markScheme: Gauss: ∮E·dA = Q/ε₀ → capacitor (C = εA/d)
Gauss for B: ∮B·dA = 0 → flux conservation in transformer/magnetic cores
Faraday: ∮E·dl = −dΦ_B/dt → transformer/generator/inductor voltage
Ampère–Maxwell: ∮B·dl = μ₀I + μ₀ε₀dΦ_E/dt → field of an inductor/solenoid, current 'through' a capacitor, EM waves
questions.modelAnswer: Gauss's law ∮ E · dA = Q_enc/ε₀ explains capacitors: it gives the field between the plates and hence C = εA/d. Gauss's law for magnetism ∮ B · dA = 0 explains why flux is conserved around a transformer core. Faraday's law ∮ E · dl = −dΦ_B/dt explains transformer and generator EMFs and the voltage L di/dt across an inductor. The Ampère–Maxwell law ∮ B · dl = μ₀I_enc + μ₀ε₀ dΦ_E/dt gives the field inside an inductor or solenoid and, through the displacement current, explains current 'passing' a capacitor and the existence of radio waves.

questions.q: Silicon at 300 K is doped with 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ phosphorus atoms. Taking n_i = 10¹⁰ cm⁻³, what is the hole concentration?
questions.why: Phosphorus is a donor, so n ≈ 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ and p = n_i²/n = 10²⁰/10¹⁶ = 10⁴ cm⁻³. 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ is the intrinsic value, ignoring the effect of doping on the minority carriers. 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ is the electron (majority) concentration. 10⁶ cm⁻³ is the ratio n/n_i, not a concentration.

questions.q: Which dopant would make silicon p-type?
questions.why: Boron is in group III, so it has one fewer valence electron than silicon and acts as an acceptor, creating holes. Phosphorus and arsenic are group V donors and make n-type material. Germanium is in group IV like silicon, so it neither donates nor accepts carriers.

questions.q: Using energy-band diagrams, explain the difference between a metal, a semiconductor and an insulator, and explain why the conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor rises with temperature.
markScheme: Metal: partially filled or overlapping bands, many free electrons
Insulator: large band gap (e.g. SiO₂ ~9 eV), negligible excitation
Semiconductor: moderate gap (e.g. Si 1.12 eV), some thermal excitation at 300 K
Excitation creates electron–hole pairs; both carry current
n_i ∝ T^(3/2) exp(−E_g/2kT) rises steeply with T, outweighing falling mobility
questions.modelAnswer: In a metal the highest occupied band is only partly filled (or bands overlap), so many electrons can gain energy from a field and conduct. In an insulator the filled valence band is separated from the empty conduction band by a large gap (about 9 eV for SiO₂), so essentially no electrons are excited and no current flows. A semiconductor has a moderate gap (1.12 eV for Si), so at room temperature some electrons are thermally excited into the conduction band, each leaving a hole; both carriers conduct. As temperature rises, the number of excited carriers n_i increases roughly as T^(3/2) exp(−E_g/2kT), an exponential increase that outweighs the modest fall in mobility, so conductivity rises (the opposite of a metal).

questions.q: Silicon is doped n-type with N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³. Taking μ_n = 1200 cm²/V s, what is its resistivity approximately?
questions.why: σ = qnμ_n = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10¹⁶ × 1200 ≈ 1.92 S/cm, so ρ = 1/σ ≈ 0.52 Ω cm. 1.9 Ω cm is the conductivity value quoted with resistivity units, i.e. forgetting to take the reciprocal. 0.0052 Ω cm is the correct value expressed in Ω m (0.0052 Ω m) but labelled in Ω cm. 3.4 × 10⁵ Ω cm is the resistivity of intrinsic silicon, ignoring the doping.

questions.q: Using the Einstein relation at 300 K, what is the electron diffusion coefficient for μ_n = 1400 cm²/V s?
questions.why: D = μkT/q = 1400 × 0.0259 ≈ 36 cm²/s. About 54,000 cm²/s divides by kT/q instead of multiplying (1400/0.0259). About 1400 cm²/s simply equates D with μ, which have different units. About 0.036 cm²/s takes kT/q as 25.9 μV rather than 25.9 mV.

questions.q: Explain the difference between drift and diffusion current. Write the total electron current density, and calculate the electron diffusion length in silicon with μ_n = 1400 cm²/V s and lifetime 1 μs at 300 K.
markScheme: Drift: carriers moved by electric field, J = qnμE
Diffusion: random thermal motion down a concentration gradient, J = qD dn/dx
Total J_n = qnμ_nE + qD_n dn/dx
questions.modelAnswer: Drift current is carried by charges pushed by an electric field; for electrons J = qnμ_nE. Diffusion current arises from random thermal motion when there is a concentration gradient, net movement being from high to low concentration; for electrons J = qD_n dn/dx. The total electron current density is J_n = qnμ_nE + qD_n dn/dx. From the Einstein relation D_n = μ_n kT/q ≈ 1400 × 0.0259 ≈ 36 cm²/s, so the diffusion length is L = √(D_nτ) = √(36 × 10⁻⁶ cm²) = 0.006 cm = 60 μm.

questions.q: An ideal silicon diode at 300 K carries 1 mA. Approximately what extra forward voltage is needed to raise the current to 100 mA?
questions.why: Each decade needs V_T ln 10 ≈ 60 mV, so two decades need about 120 mV. About 60 mV is the figure for a single decade (×10, not ×100). About 180 mV counts 1 mA to 100 mA as three decades instead of two. About 26 mV is V_T itself, which multiplies the current by e, not by 100.

questions.q: For a silicon junction with N_A = 10¹⁷ cm⁻³, N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ and n_i = 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ at 300 K, the built-in potential is closest to:
questions.why: V_bi = 0.0259 × ln(10¹⁷ × 10¹⁶/10²⁰) = 0.0259 × ln(10¹³) ≈ 0.0259 × 29.9 ≈ 0.77 V. 0.36 V is kT ln(N_D/n_i), only the n-side Fermi-level shift, missing the p-side contribution. 1.12 V is the band gap, which is an upper bound for non-degenerate doping, not the built-in potential. 0.60 V is the rule-of-thumb forward 'turn-on' voltage, a different quantity.

questions.q: Describe how the depletion region and built-in field form at a p–n junction in equilibrium, and explain qualitatively why forward bias produces an exponentially increasing current while reverse bias gives only a small saturation current.
markScheme: Diffusion of majority carriers across junction; recombination leaves ionised dopants
Space charge (−ve on p side, +ve on n side) creates field n → p and barrier V_bi
Equilibrium: drift balances diffusion, no net current
Forward bias lowers barrier; number of carriers able to cross ∝ exp(qV/kT) (Boltzmann)
Reverse bias raises barrier; only thermally generated minority carriers drift across → small I_S
questions.modelAnswer: On contact, electrons diffuse from n to p and holes from p to n, recombining near the junction. This uncovers fixed negative acceptor ions on the p side and positive donor ions on the n side, a depletion region with a field pointing from n to p and a potential barrier V_bi. In equilibrium the drift current due to this field exactly cancels the diffusion current. Forward bias reduces the barrier by V; because carrier energies follow a Boltzmann distribution, the number with enough energy to cross rises as exp(qV/kT), so diffusion current grows exponentially. Reverse bias increases the barrier, stopping majority diffusion; only the few thermally generated minority carriers near the junction are swept across by the field, giving a small, nearly voltage-independent current I_S.

questions.q: An LED is made from a direct-gap semiconductor with E_g = 1.9 eV. Its emission wavelength is closest to:
questions.why: λ ≈ 1240/1.9 ≈ 653 nm, which is red. 1.9 μm simply reuses the number 1.9 as micrometres. 470 nm (blue) corresponds to about 2.6 eV, a larger gap. 2360 nm multiplies 1240 by 1.9 instead of dividing.

questions.q: A 1 cm² solar cell under 100 mW/cm² has V_oc = 0.6 V, I_sc = 35 mA and fill factor 0.8. What is its efficiency?
questions.why: P_max = FF × V_oc × I_sc = 0.8 × 0.6 × 35 mA = 16.8 mW, so η = 16.8/100 = 16.8 %. 21 % leaves out the fill factor (0.6 × 35 = 21 mW). 13.4 % applies the fill factor twice (0.8² × 21). 26.3 % divides by the fill factor instead of multiplying (21/0.8).

questions.q: Explain how a p–n junction solar cell converts light into electrical power, including the role of the band gap and the built-in field, and calculate V_oc for I_L = 35 mA and I_0 = 10⁻¹² A at 300 K.
markScheme: Photons with E > E_g create electron–hole pairs; sub-gap photons not absorbed; excess energy lost as heat
Built-in field in depletion region separates pairs: electrons to n, holes to p
Carriers generated within a diffusion length can reach the junction and be collected
Photocurrent flows through external load; cell works in fourth quadrant (forward voltage, current out)
questions.modelAnswer: Photons with energy above the band gap are absorbed, each creating an electron–hole pair; photons below E_g pass through and any energy above E_g is lost as heat. Pairs generated in the depletion region, or within about a diffusion length of it, are separated by the built-in field, electrons going to the n side and holes to the p side. This charge separation drives a photocurrent through an external load while the junction develops a forward voltage, so the device delivers power. At open circuit, the photocurrent is balanced by forward diode current: V_oc = V_T ln(I_L/I_0 + 1) = 0.0259 × ln(3.5 × 10¹⁰) ≈ 0.0259 × 24.3 ≈ 0.63 V.

questions.q: An n-MOSFET has μ_nC_ox = 200 μA/V², W/L = 10, V_T = 0.5 V, V_GS = 1.5 V and V_DS = 2 V. What is I_D?
questions.why: V_DS = 2 V exceeds V_GS − V_T = 1 V, so the device is in saturation: I_D = ½ × 200 μA/V² × 10 × (1 V)² = 1 mA. 2 mA omits the factor ½. 0 mA applies the triode formula even though V_DS > V_GS − V_T: (1 × 2 − 2²/2) = 0, a sign that the wrong region was assumed. 2.25 mA uses V_GS² instead of (V_GS − V_T)², ignoring the threshold.

questions.q: In an npn BJT in forward-active mode with β = 100 and I_B = 20 μA, what is the emitter current?
questions.why: I_C = βI_B = 2.00 mA, and I_E = I_C + I_B = 2.00 + 0.02 = 2.02 mA. 2.00 mA is the collector current, not the emitter current. 20 μA is the base current. 1.98 mA subtracts the base current instead of adding it.

questions.q: Explain how an n-channel enhancement MOSFET forms a conducting channel and why its drain current saturates. Calculate g_m for μ_nC_ox = 200 μA/V², W/L = 10, V_T = 0.5 V and V_GS = 1.5 V in saturation.
markScheme: Positive gate voltage on MOS capacitor attracts electrons, repels holes; above V_T surface inverts to n-type channel
Channel charge per area ≈ C_ox(V_GS − V_T); gate insulated so no DC gate current
As V_DS rises to V_GS − V_T the channel pinches off at the drain end; further V_DS drops across pinch-off region so I_D ≈ constant
g_m = 2I_D/(V_GS − V_T) = 2 mS (or μ_nC_ox(W/L)(V_GS − V_T))
questions.modelAnswer: The gate, oxide and p-type silicon form a capacitor. A positive gate voltage pushes holes away from the surface and attracts electrons; once V_GS exceeds the threshold V_T, the surface inverts to n-type and a channel of mobile electrons, with charge per area about C_ox(V_GS − V_T), connects source and drain. Increasing V_DS raises current until V_DS = V_GS − V_T, when the channel charge at the drain end falls to zero (pinch-off). Extra drain voltage is then dropped across the pinched-off region and I_D stays nearly constant: saturation. Here I_D = ½ × 200 × 10⁻⁶ × 10 × 1² = 1 mA and g_m = μ_nC_ox(W/L)(V_GS − V_T) = 2 × 10⁻³ × 1 = 2 mS, equal to 2I_D/(V_GS − V_T).

questions.q:
(a) Write down Maxwell's four equations in integral form for vacuum and state the physical meaning of each. [6]
(b) Use Gauss's law to find the capacitance of a MOS gate of area 1 μm² with a 10 nm SiO₂ layer (ε_r ≈ 3.9). State your assumptions. [5]
(c) The capacitor is charged by a constant 1 nA current. Show that the displacement current between the plates equals 1 nA, and find dE/dt in the oxide. [5]
(d) A 100-turn pickup coil of area 10 cm² is near a conductor whose field changes from 0.5 T to 0 in 10 ms. Find the induced EMF and give its direction rule. [4]
markScheme: (a) Gauss ∮E·dA = Q/ε₀ (charge sources E); ∮B·dA = 0 (no monopoles)
(a) Faraday ∮E·dl = −dΦ_B/dt (changing B induces E); Ampère–Maxwell ∮B·dl = μ₀I + μ₀ε₀dΦ_E/dt (currents and changing E produce B)
(b) Pillbox, uniform field, no fringing: C = ε₀ε_rA/d ≈ 3.45 fF
(c) ε dΦ_E/dt = εA dE/dt = dQ/dt = I = 1 nA (with ε = ε₀ε_r in the oxide)
(c) dE/dt = I/(ε₀ε_rA) ≈ 10⁻⁹/(3.45 × 10⁻²³) ≈ 2.9 × 10¹³ V/m per s
(d) Lenz's law: induced current opposes the decrease, i.e. tries to maintain the original flux
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Gauss's law ∮ E · dA = Q_enc/ε₀: the net outward electric flux through a closed surface measures the enclosed charge; charges are the sources of E. Gauss's law for magnetism ∮ B · dA = 0: no magnetic monopoles, so B lines form closed loops. Faraday's law ∮ E · dl = −dΦ_B/dt: a changing magnetic flux induces a circulating electric field (EMF). Ampère–Maxwell law ∮ B · dl = μ₀I_enc + μ₀ε₀ dΦ_E/dt: conduction currents and changing electric flux produce a circulating magnetic field.

(b) Assume the gate is large compared with the oxide thickness so the field is uniform and fringing is negligible, and the silicon behaves as the second plate. A pillbox through the gate gives D = σ, so E = σ/(ε₀ε_r) and V = Ed. Then C = Q/V = ε₀ε_rA/d = 3.9 × 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 10⁻¹²/10⁻⁸ ≈ 3.45 × 10⁻¹⁵ F ≈ 3.5 fF.

(c) Inside the oxide, E = Q/(ε₀ε_rA). The displacement current through a surface between the plates is ε₀ε_r dΦ_E/dt = ε₀ε_rA dE/dt = dQ/dt, which is the 1 nA charging current in the leads. (In a dielectric the displacement current density is dD/dt.) Hence dE/dt = I/(ε₀ε_rA) = 10⁻⁹/(3.45 × 10⁻²³) ≈ 2.9 × 10¹³ V/m per second; equivalently dV/dt = I/C ≈ 2.9 × 10⁵ V/s, so it takes only a few microseconds to reach 1 V.

(d) Flux change per turn = AΔB = 10⁻³ × 0.5 = 5 × 10⁻⁴ Wb over 0.01 s, so |ε| = 100 × 5 × 10⁻⁴/0.01 = 5 V. By Lenz's law the induced current flows in the sense that would create flux in the original direction of B, opposing its decrease.

questions.q:
Silicon at 300 K (n_i = 10¹⁰ cm⁻³, kT/q = 25.9 mV).
(a) An n-type region has N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³. Find n, p and the resistivity, taking μ_n = 1200 cm²/V s. [5]
(b) It forms a junction with p-type material, N_A = 10¹⁷ cm⁻³. Find V_bi and state which side the depletion region mainly occupies, with a reason. [5]
(c) The diode has I_S = 10⁻¹⁴ A. Find the current at 0.60 V and 0.70 V and comment on the ratio. [5]
(d) The same junction is used as a 1 cm² solar cell with I_L = 35 mA and I_0 = 10⁻¹² A. Find V_oc, and the efficiency under 100 mW/cm² if FF = 0.8. [5]
markScheme: (a) n ≈ N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³; p = n_i²/n = 10⁴ cm⁻³
(a) σ = qnμ_n ≈ 1.92 S/cm; ρ ≈ 0.52 Ω cm
(b) Mainly on the n side (lighter doping); N_A x_p = N_D x_n so x_n = 10 x_p
(c) Ratio ≈ e^(0.1/0.0259) ≈ 48: 100 mV ≈ 1.7 decades (60 mV/decade)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Donors are fully ionised, so n ≈ N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³. Mass action gives p = n_i²/n = 10²⁰/10¹⁶ = 10⁴ cm⁻³. The hole contribution to conductivity is negligible, so σ = qnμ_n = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10¹⁶ × 1200 ≈ 1.92 S/cm and ρ = 1/σ ≈ 0.52 Ω cm.

(b) V_bi = (kT/q) ln(N_A N_D/n_i²) = 0.0259 × ln(10¹⁷ × 10¹⁶/10²⁰) = 0.0259 × ln(10¹³) = 0.0259 × 29.93 ≈ 0.77 V. Charge neutrality requires equal and opposite depletion charge on each side, N_A x_p = N_D x_n, so x_n/x_p = N_A/N_D = 10: about 90 % of the depletion width lies on the more lightly doped n side.

(c) With n = 1: I(0.60) = 10⁻¹⁴ × [exp(0.60/0.0259) − 1] = 10⁻¹⁴ × e^(23.17) ≈ 1.15 × 10⁻⁴ A = 0.115 mA. I(0.70) = 10⁻¹⁴ × e^(27.03) ≈ 5.5 × 10⁻³ A = 5.5 mA. The ratio is exp(0.1/0.0259) ≈ 48, so a 100 mV increase raises the current about 48-fold, consistent with about 60 mV per decade. This steepness is why a silicon diode looks as if it 'turns on' at about 0.6–0.7 V.

(d) V_oc = V_T ln(I_L/I_0 + 1) = 0.0259 × ln(3.5 × 10¹⁰) = 0.0259 × 24.28 ≈ 0.63 V. Taking I_sc ≈ I_L = 35 mA, P_max = FF × V_oc × I_sc = 0.8 × 0.63 × 35 ≈ 17.6 mW. With 100 mW incident on 1 cm², η ≈ 17.6 %.
